text: A Priority 1 incident and a Major Incident get confused constantly, but they are not the same thing. Priority 1 says this incident is Critical by the Impact and Urgency matrix from the last lesson. Major Incident Management is a separate, heavier process reserved for incidents that cross a severity threshold the organization defines in advance, not just a label attached to any Critical ticket.

Modern instances track that with a real field, major_incident_state, distinct from the ordinary state field on the incident record. Its values are typically None, Candidate, and Declared. Keeping it as its own field, separate from Priority and State, is what lets an incident stay Priority 1 in the ordinary sense while a completely different workflow — notifications, a major incident manager role, a bridge — spins up around it only once Declared.

Hitting the threshold should make an incident a Candidate, not automatically Declared. A human, usually a major incident manager or on-call lead, reviews it and makes the actual call — because automatic declaration produces false positives, like a Priority 1 affecting one VIP user, and erodes trust in the process the first time it fires for something that didn't truly need it.

Once declared, a Major Incident runs on practices a standard incident doesn't. A dedicated war room or bridge call pulls the right people together in real time instead of ticket-comment handoffs, and stakeholder communication moves to a fixed cadence — updates every 15 or 30 minutes to leadership and affected business units, instead of the ad hoc updates a normal incident's comments provide.

A Major Incident also carries a requirement standard incidents don't: a formal post-incident review after resolution, documenting the timeline, what worked, what didn't, and what changes should follow — on top of the ordinary Resolution Code and Close Notes.
